steps.body: A table or a list of (input, output) pairs is a function when no input appears twice with different outputs. Scan the input column: if every input value is paired with just one output, it's a function.
Sweep one input at a time and count how many outputs it reaches.

widget.prompt: Sweep across the discrete relation. Find the repeated input that reaches two different outputs, then decide whether the relation is a function.
widget.successFeedback: Not a function. At least one input lines up with two outputs, so the one-output promise is broken.
widget.moreSweepFeedback: Sweep farther across the inputs. One repeated input with two output points is enough to disprove the function claim.
widget.verdictFeedback: Count outputs while the scanner fixes one input. Any count above one means the relation is not a function.

predict.prompt: Which situation breaks the definition of a function?

options.label: One input paired with different outputs
Different inputs sharing one output
Either situation breaks it

predict.reveal: A function assigns exactly one output to each input. Several inputs may share an output, but one input cannot point to two different outputs.

steps.body: The rule fails when the SAME input shows two different outputs. In (1, 2), (1, 5), the input 1 appears twice — once giving 2, once giving 5 — so it's not a function. Repeated inputs are the red flag to look for.

explanationVariants: Input 4 appears twice — once with 1, once with 9 — so it's NOT a function.
The same input (4) giving two different outputs breaks the one-output rule.

options.label: No — input 4 appears twice with different outputs
options.feedback: Right — 4 → 1 and 4 → 9 breaks the one-output rule.

options.label: Yes — all the pairs are listed clearly
options.feedback: Being clearly listed doesn't make it a function — input 4 has TWO outputs (1 and 9), so it fails.

options.label: Yes — the outputs are all different
options.feedback: Different outputs would be fine if inputs were unique, but input 4 repeats with different outputs — not a function.

options.label: Only if 4 comes first
options.feedback: Order doesn't matter — input 4 appears twice with different outputs no matter the order.

options.label: Yes — each input appears exactly once
options.feedback: Right — inputs 1, 2, 3 are all unique; sharing output 8 doesn't break anything.

options.label: No — the output 8 repeats
options.feedback: Repeated OUTPUTS are allowed — only repeated INPUTS with different outputs break the rule.

options.label: No — every output should be different
options.feedback: Functions don't require unique outputs — many inputs can share one output.

options.label: Only if the inputs also repeated
options.feedback: Repeated inputs would actually risk breaking it — unique inputs like these are exactly what a function needs.

explanationVariants: Input 2 appears twice with different outputs (5 and 8), so the table is NOT a function.
The repeated input 2 giving two outputs breaks the one-output rule.

widget.prompt: A table has inputs 1, 2, 3, 2 with outputs 4, 5, 6, 8. Is it a function?

options.label: No — input 2 appears twice with outputs 5 and 8
options.feedback: Right — 2 → 5 and 2 → 8 breaks the one-output rule.

options.label: Yes — there are four pairs
options.feedback: Count isn't the test — input 2 repeats with different outputs, so it fails.

options.label: Yes — the outputs are all different
options.feedback: The outputs being different doesn't help — input 2 maps to two of them, breaking the rule.

options.label: Only if you remove input 1
options.feedback: Removing input 1 wouldn't fix the input-2 repeat, which is the actual problem.

steps.body: A table with a partial repeat.
explanationVariants: Each input (2, 5, 9) appears exactly once, so the table is a function — even though two outputs (7) match.
Unique inputs mean it's a function; the outputs matching for two of them doesn't matter.

widget.prompt: A table has inputs 2, 5, 9 with outputs 7, 7, 3. Is it a function?

options.label: Yes — inputs 2, 5, 9 are each listed once
options.feedback: Right — every input is unique; outputs 7 and 7 matching for two of them is allowed.

options.label: No — the output 7 repeats
options.feedback: Repeated OUTPUTS are allowed — only a repeated INPUT with different outputs breaks the rule, and no input here repeats.

options.label: No — a table function needs every output to differ
options.feedback: Functions don't require different outputs — two inputs may share one, as 2 and 5 do here.

options.label: Only if 9 also had output 7
options.feedback: The rule doesn't need ALL outputs to match — 2 and 5 sharing 7 while 9 has 3 is still perfectly fine.

steps.body: Sort tables into functions and non-functions.
explanationVariants: Functions have every input appearing once; non-functions repeat an input with different outputs. Scan the input column of each.
The single test is whether any input value shows up twice with different outputs.

widget.prompt: Sort each set of pairs: function or not?

items.feedback: Inputs 1, 2, 3 are all unique — a function (shared output is fine).
Input 5 appears twice with outputs 1 and 2 — not a function.
Inputs 0, 1, 2 are all unique — a function.
Input 7 appears twice with outputs 8 and 9 — not a function.
Inputs 2, 4, 6 are all unique — a function (shared output 5 is fine).

widget.missFeedback: Not quite — scan each input column for a value that repeats with different outputs.
widget.successFeedback: All sorted — a set is a function exactly when no input repeats with different outputs.

hints: For each set, look only at the INPUT (first) numbers — does any repeat?
If an input repeats, check whether its two outputs differ. Same output twice is still fine.

steps.body: A table or list of pairs is a function when no input repeats with different outputs.
takeaways: Scan the INPUT column for repeats.
A repeated input with different outputs means it's NOT a function.
Repeated outputs across different inputs are always fine.
steps.teaser: Next: the vertical line test — spotting functions on a graph.

concept.body: A list of pairs is a function when no input value repeats with two different outputs. Scan the input column: repeated inputs with different outputs break the rule; repeated outputs are fine.

explanationVariants: Input 3 appears twice with outputs 1 and 2, so it's NOT a function.
The repeated input 3 with two outputs breaks the one-output rule.

options.label: No — input 3 appears twice with different outputs
options.feedback: Right — 3 → 1 and 3 → 2 breaks the rule.

options.label: Yes — there are three pairs
options.feedback: Count isn't the test — input 3 repeats with different outputs.

options.label: Yes — the outputs differ
options.feedback: Different outputs don't help when the same INPUT (3) maps to two of them.

options.label: Only if 3 appeared once
options.feedback: Exactly — and since it appears twice with different outputs, it's not a function.
